> 未濟。亨。小狐汔濟，濡其尾，無攸利。

The last hexagram in the book is about not having finished, and that is where the 易 ends on purpose.

## 未: branches still growing

未: the oracle-bone form is a tree with layered, still-growing branches; 說文 glosses it 未，味也，六月，滋味也，象木重枝葉也.

Original sense: the branches are still putting out leaves. Borrowed for "not."

And the distinction is worth a sentence: this "not" is not a refusal. It is "not yet."

未濟 is "the crossing is not finished," not "the crossing cannot be made."

One character, and the whole tone of the hexagram is set: it is a progress bar, not a verdict.

## 汔: almost, and not yet

汛: originally water dried up (說文 汔，水涸也); borrowed for 幾 — 詩 汔可小康, "almost able to rest."

So 汔 is the state of nearly-but-not-yet.

小狐汔濟，濡其尾 — the small fox is nearly across, and its tail gets wet.

The 易 chose this character for exactly that distance — the stretch that is hardest to bear, the last few steps where the wet tail happens.

Which is the hexagram's whole argument: the last part of the crossing is the part where everything goes wrong, and the small fox is the one who tries it at full speed.

## 曳其輪

Nine-two: pull back on the wheel; keeping to it is good.

The same gesture as 既濟初九, in the opposite hexagram, and with the same logic: in the place that is not finished, the useful act is braking. Speed is what wets the tail.

## 未濟，征凶，利涉大川

Six-three says both: not yet across; advancing is bad; it is fitting to cross the great river.

Which looks like a contradiction and is not. It is the exact structure of the unfinished: do not push from here, and the river still has to be crossed.

So 未濟 has no advice that resolves. It has a condition and a direction.

## 震用伐鬼方，三年有賞于大國

Nine-four: using 震 to campaign against the Gui region, three years, and a reward from the great state.

三年 for the second time in the book, and the advice is the same as 既濟九三's: the biggest work is measured in years, not in pushes.

## 君子之光，有孚

Six-five: 貞吉，無悔，君子之光，有孚，吉.

And the 象 that goes with it: 君子之光，其暉吉也.

暉: light, and specifically light that reaches sideways to others (說文 暉，光也).

Which is the chapter's most careful distinction: 光 is one's own brightness. 暉 is brightness arriving on someone else.

So six-five is judged good not for how bright it is, but for who it lit.

## 有孚于飲酒，無咎；濡其首，有孚失是

Top line: trust in drinking wine, no fault; but wet the head, and the trust loses 是.

是: originally "straight" (說文 是，直也), extended to "correct," "this."

And the reading has to be the first one: losing 是 is losing the correct, not "losing this."

Which is the last sentence of the sixty-four: the celebration at the end of the crossing is allowed — pour the wine, no fault — and the line that ends the book is the one where the head goes under.

A hexagram about not-yet-finished ends with a warning about finishing too early, in drink.

## 慎辨物居方

The 象: 君子以慎辨物居方.

方: originally two boats lashed together (說文 方，並船也), extended to position, place.

居方: each thing in its own place.

Which is the final instruction of the whole book: distinguish the things, and put each where it belongs. Not "complete the crossing." Place things.

## The test

The last hexagram asks the first question of the whole series: what is not yet finished in what you are doing, and are you going at it like the small fox — at full speed, near the bank, with the tail already wet?
